parameters.name: Oxygen consumed per astronaut
parameters.note: Nominal metabolic O₂ consumption for an average crew member.

parameters.name: Water used per astronaut
parameters.note: Drinking, food rehydration and minimal hygiene. Full hygiene and laundry would need much more.

parameters.name: Water recovery rate
parameters.note: ISS Water Recovery System; 98% with the Brine Processor Assembly (2023).

parameters.name: Water needed per kg of O₂ (electrolysis)
parameters.note: Stoichiometry of 2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + O₂ (18 g water per 16 g O₂).

parameters.name: Radiation dose on the lunar surface (GCR)
parameters.note: Dose equivalent measured by Chang'e-4 LND: 1369 µSv/day. Habitat walls reduce it modestly (game factor 0.7).

parameters.name: Short-term radiation limit (30 days, blood-forming organs)
parameters.note: Used as the mission-failure threshold (treated as mSv for simplicity).

parameters.name: Solar storm dose inside a thin habitat
parameters.note: Game estimate for an S3 storm; large historical events (e.g. August 1972) could have delivered far more behind thin shielding.

parameters.name: Shelter storm-dose reduction
parameters.note: Order-of-magnitude reduction for ~20–30 g/cm² of regolith or water against solar-proton spectra.

parameters.name: Li-ion battery specific energy
parameters.note: 60 kWh module = 250 kg in the game.

parameters.note: Artemis crews are planned around four astronauts.

oxygen.title: The crew ran out of oxygen
oxygen.what: The oxygen stored in the base reached zero.
oxygen.why: Four astronauts breathe about 3.4 kg of oxygen every day. Oxygen tanks are heavy, and the oxygen generator needs both water and power to make more.
oxygen.principle: Life support is a chain: oxygen depends on water, and making oxygen depends on power. If any link breaks, the whole chain fails.
alternatives: Bring more oxygen tanks, or an oxygen generator for longer missions
Keep the oxygen generator powered — don't let it be the first thing shed
Carry spare parts so a broken generator can be fixed
A greenhouse adds a little oxygen as a backup

water.title: The base ran out of water
water.why: Water is used for drinking, food, hygiene — and to make oxygen and grow plants. Without recycling, every drop used is gone.
water.principle: Closing the loop: recycling 93% of water means you need about 14 times less water from Earth. The longer the mission, the more recycling pays off.
alternatives: Bring a water recycler — on long missions it's lighter than the water it saves
Fix leaks quickly instead of letting them run
Watch the oxygen generator: it turns water into oxygen

food.title: The crew ran out of food
food.what: Food stores stayed empty for several days and mission control ordered an abort.
food.why: Four astronauts eat about 7 kg of packaged food a day. A greenhouse takes a week to produce its first harvest and only covers part of the need.
food.principle: Plan for growth time: biological systems take days or weeks to start producing, so stored food must bridge the gap.
alternatives: Bring enough food crates to cover the days before the first harvest
Keep the greenhouse powered and healthy
Don't count on the greenhouse alone — it's a supplement, not a full supply

power.title: Critical power failure
power.what: The batteries were empty and the solar arrays couldn't power the habitat's core life support for several days.
power.why: When solar generation drops — in shadow, or with dusty panels — the base lives on stored energy. Once batteries run dry, heating, air circulation and CO₂ removal stop.
power.principle: Energy storage must cover critical loads during the longest expected period of low generation, with a safety margin.
alternatives: Bring more battery modules to cover the shadow period
Add solar arrays so batteries recharge faster in sunlight
Switch off non-essential systems (greenhouse first) before the shadow arrives
Clean dusty panels quickly

radiation.title: Radiation dose exceeded the safety limit
radiation.what: The crew's radiation dose passed 250 mSv, NASA's short-term safety limit. Mission control ordered an emergency return.
radiation.why: The Moon has no magnetic field or thick atmosphere. During a solar storm, the dose inside a thin-walled habitat can rise to tens of mSv per day.
radiation.principle: Radiation protection = time + distance + shielding. You can't control the Sun, so you need mass (regolith, water) between the crew and the storm.
alternatives: Bring a radiation shelter and use it during storms
Keep at least 100 kg of water to build a water wall if you have no shelter
Don't continue normal operations during a severe storm

successLesson.title: Mission accomplished!
successLesson.what: Your crew survived the whole mission and the base kept running.
successLesson.why: You balanced power, water, oxygen, food and radiation protection — even when the storm and the shadow hit.
successLesson.principle: Mission design is about trade-offs: every kilogram and every kilowatt-hour spent on one system is not available for another.
alternatives: Try the mission again with a lighter loadout
Try a different choice during the solar storm and compare the dose
Take on the Commander mission: 28 days at Artemis Base Camp
